item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating immediate intent from persistent preference. [LSIDN (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14743) uses distinct encoders and denoising strategies: session-level interest extraction/evolution for long-term preferences, contrastive augmentation for short-term interests. [TLSTSRec (2024 online; 2025 issue)](https://doi.org/10.3233/IDA-240051) models temporal duration and spectrum, then adaptively fuses long- and short-term representations. [CoVE (2025; revised January 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23170) dynamically combines specialized recommendation experts. Together, these suggest testing a recent-history encoder plus a persistent-preference branch, with learned fusion conditioned on available history and time gaps; improvement on this benchmark remains unverified.\n\nMulti-interest modeling offers another useful distinction. [ULIM (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10097) partitions histories into category-aware interest subsequences and models long- and short-term interests within each cluster. Its category supervision is unavailable here; learned latent interest slots would be an adaptation. Complementarity requires particular caution: [KGSCL (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089360802500070X) uses explicit substitution/complementarity relationships from Amazon metadata, which this task does not supply. A feasible experimental alternative is a directional transition branch learned only from training histories, alongside preference similarity and recent intent. Treat its patterns as predictive associations, without claiming observed purchase purposes or true complementarity. Compare branch ablations using the pinned macro validation HR@10 across all four categories."}
